title: Describing people: personality and character traits
subtitle: impetuous, taciturn, aloof, gullible
summary: Name personality types precisely - impetuous, effusive, diffident, aloof, gullible - and switch between the adjective and its abstract noun.

lesson.heading: Adjectives for personality and behaviour
rows: acts on a sudden idea without thinking first (often negative)
similar to impetuous, but can be used more positively
gives exaggerated expression of pleasure, praise or gratitude
always selfishly promoting your own position or interests (informal)
nervous or uncomfortable because you know what people think of you
calm and reasonable and showing good judgement
reserved or says very little (generally negative)

lesson.heading: Using those adjectives
lesson.text: **Impetuous** and **impulsive** both describe acting on a sudden idea, but **impetuous** usually criticises, while **impulsive** can be warm. Do not confuse **conscientious** (taking your work seriously) with **self-conscious** (uncomfortably aware of what others think).

examples.text: She's so **impetuous**; I wish she would consider things before acting.
His **impulsive** generosity led him to give money to anyone who asked for help.
She always gives me such an **effusive** welcome when I visit her.
Freddie seemed **self-conscious** and uncomfortable when he had to make the announcement.
He was a bit **taciturn** when I first met him. He hardly said a word.

lesson.heading: Sociable or not

left.label: Sociable
examples: Her brother Mark is so **outgoing** and is such an **extrovert**.
Joe is always so polite and **respectful**.

right.label: Unsociable
examples: Chloe's such an **introvert** - inward-looking and quiet.
English people are traditionally thought of as rather **reserved**.
Eva tends to be rather **aloof**. I don't know if she's just shy.
I've always found Professor Mactoft very **unapproachable**.

lesson.note: Reserved means not immediately sociable; aloof is stronger and means unfriendly.

lesson.heading: Confidence, high and low
lesson.text: A **diffident** person lacks confidence and may have low **self-esteem** - a low opinion of themselves. At the other extreme, a **conceited** person thinks they are wonderful and a **self-important** one has an exaggerated sense of their own importance. A **modest** person prefers not to exaggerate their own qualities.

examples.text: Mr Rogers is such a **diffident** man. He seems to have quite low **self-esteem**.
Natasha is very **conceited** and **self-important**, but Rachel is such a **modest** person.
Don't be so **conceited**! You're not the only one to get an A-grade!

lesson.heading: Looking down on others
lesson.text: Someone **haughty** is unfriendly and thinks themselves better than others; someone **disdainful** does not believe others deserve respect. These are strong, critical words, so use them carefully.

examples.text: My aunt Annie can be very **haughty** and **disdainful** at times, but she's lovely really.
At times, Joel is quite **haughty** and acts as if he's better than the rest of us.
Frances was very **aloof** at the party and would not take part in things.

lesson.heading: Character traits
lesson.text: A **naive** person is willing to believe simple things, perhaps because of inexperience; a **gullible** person is easily deceived. A **restless** person is never satisfied with what they are doing now. **Obstinate** means unwilling to change despite persuasion, and **pig-headed** is a stronger, informal version of it.

examples.text: Arjen is a somewhat **naive** person; he thinks love can solve all the world's problems.
Telephone salespeople often take advantage of **gullible** people.
She's a **restless** individual. I don't think she'll ever settle down in a job.
You are so **obstinate** and **pig-headed**! Why don't you listen when people give you advice?
My father was a very **conscientious** man; he never took time off work unless he was really sick.

lesson.text: Conscientious = hard-working and careful. Self-conscious = awkward because people are watching. The two are easily mixed up.

exercises.prompt: What is a stronger and less formal way of saying obstinate?
exercises.explanation: Pig-headed is a stronger, informal version of obstinate.

exercises.prompt: If someone is diffident, they have ___ self-confidence.
exercises.explanation: A diffident person lacks confidence and often has low self-esteem.

exercises.prompt: Which adjective describes a greeting that shows exaggerated pleasure?
exercises.explanation: An effusive welcome gives exaggerated expression of pleasure or gratitude.

exercises.prompt: Which word would most people rather be described as?
exercises.explanation: Conscientious means always taking your work seriously; self-conscious means uncomfortably aware of others' opinions.

exercises.prompt: If you're outgoing, you are more likely to be seen as ___.
exercises.explanation: An extrovert is outward-looking, energetic and sociable.

exercises.prompt: People who have low ___ can find it difficult to achieve their goals.
exercises.explanation: Low self-esteem means having a low opinion of yourself.

exercises.prompt: He's generally an ___ sort of person - happy and sociable.
exercises.explanation: Outgoing means energetic and friendly, finding it easy to be with others.

exercises.prompt: She is a ___ person overall - calm, reasonable and sensible.
exercises.explanation: Well-balanced means calm and reasonable and showing good judgement.

exercises.prompt: You always seem ___. What's the problem? You never settle to anything.
exercises.explanation: A restless person is not satisfied with what they are doing now and wants something new.

exercises.prompt: He's so ___. He should try to calm down more.
exercises.explanation: An excitable person is easily excited by things.

exercises.prompt: She is rather ___ when it comes to politics - she believes rather simple things.
exercises.explanation: Naive means willing to believe simple things, perhaps because of inexperience.

exercises.prompt: He's ___ and cares little what happens to others - he just pursues his own interests.
exercises.explanation: Pushy means always selfishly promoting your own position or interests.

exercises.prompt: One of her main character traits is ___.
exercises.explanation: The noun from impetuous is impetuosity (or, less commonly, impetuousness).

exercises.prompt: Online identity thieves prey on people's ___.
exercises.explanation: Gullibility is the quality of being easily deceived.

exercises.prompt: ___ seems to be a family trait among my relatives - nobody will ever change their mind.
exercises.explanation: The noun from pig-headed is pig-headedness.

exercises.prompt: Match each adjective with its abstract noun.

exercises.statement: It would be difficult to have a friendly conversation with a taciturn person.
exercises.explanation: Correct - a taciturn person is reserved and says very little.

exercises.statement: An unapproachable boss is one that you can easily talk to.
exercises.explanation: That is an approachable boss. Unapproachable means not easy to be sociable with or start a conversation with.

exercises.prompt: Is each adjective mainly complimentary or mainly critical?

exercises.answer: Why don't you listen when people give you advice?
exercises.explanation: This is what you say to someone who is obstinate and pig-headed.
